figures.caption: Table 1. Summary of the mathematical models used to generate synthetic training data. The test cases are arranged in order of increasing mechanistic complexity. ADR, advection–diffusion–reaction.

Fig 1. Overview of the ADR–BINN framework and representative output. Top: Schematic of the BINN architecture used to learn the constitutive operators in the general advection–diffusion–reaction equation (Eq. (1)). The solution network uθ(x, t) is trained from noisy observations and evaluated at randomly sampled collocation points. The predicted solution is then passed to the operator networks Dϕ(u), Vζ(u), and Gψ(u), with automatic differentiation used to compute the PDE residual. The data, PDE, and boundary-condition losses are combined to form the total loss used for joint optimisation of all four networks. Bottom: Representative ADR–BINN outputs and reconstruction for the nonlinear reaction–diffusion–advection benchmark (Eq. (13)) with additive Gaussian noise of variance σ2 = 0.001. Shown are the learned solution uθ(x, t) (blue), and the forward-predicted solution up(x, t) (orange) plotted at the temporal resolution described in Table 4, and the learned constitutive functions Dϕ(u) (green), Gψ(u) (purple), and Vζ(u) (brown). Dashed black curves denote the true solution or constitutive functions, coloured lines show the output from one single BINN initialisation. The forward-predicted solution is obtained by numerically solving Eq. (1) using the learned operators and learned initial condition. More details can be found in the Supporting Material. The ADR–BINN hyperparameters take the default values given in Table 3.
Table 2. Variables used throughout the ADR–BINN framework. SoftplusReLU(x) = log(1 + ex) for x < 20, and SoftplusReLU(x) = max(0, x) otherwise.

Table 3. Default hyperparameters used throughout the ADR–BINN framework. Network parameters are learned during training; the remaining default values were determined from preliminary numerical investigations.

Fig 2. Effect of additive Gaussian noise on BINN performance in the linear diffusion equation (Eq. (3)). Left: Learned solution uθ(x, t) (top), learned diffusivity Dϕ(u) (middle), and forward-predicted solution up(x, t) (bottom, plotted for t = tend as specified in Table 4). Results are for a representative ADR–BINN trained with additive Gaussian noise of variance σ2 = 0.001 and (hu, nh) = (4, 32). Dashed black lines denote the true solution or constitutive function, coloured lines denote the mean over ten independent BINN initialisations, and shaded regions indicate ±1 standard deviation. Right: Relative L2 errors in the learned solution uθ(x, t) (top) and predicted solution up(x, t) (middle), as a function of the observation noise variance for the architectures (hu, nu) = (4, 32) and (6, 128). Boxplots summarise ten BINN initialisations for each of ten independently generated datasets. The botto plot shows the total validation loss during training for representative combinations of architecture and noise levels. Unless stated otherwise, all remaining ADR–BINN hyperparameters take the default values given in Table 3.

Fig 3. Effect of the learning rate, r, on BINNs performance on data simulated from the Burgers’ equation (10) with additive Gaussian noise of variance σ2 = 0.001. Top: Learned solution uθ(x, t) (left) and forward-predicted solution up(x, t) (right) plotted at the time resolution described in Table 4. Middle: Learned diffusivity Dϕ(u) (left) and advection velocity Vζ(u) (right). Results correspond to the representative learning rate r = 5× 10−4 (top); dashed black curves denote the true operators and shaded regions indicate ±1 standard deviation over ten independent ADR–BINN initialisations. Bottom: Total validation loss (left) and relative L2 errors in uθ and up (right) for various learning rates, r. Unless stated otherwise, all remaining ADR–BINN hyperparameters take the default values given in Table 3.

Fig 4. Effect of the PDE residual weighting wPDE on BINN performance for the porous-medium equation (Eq. (6)) with additive Gaussian noise of variance σ2 = 0.001, whilst wdata = 1 and wBC = 0. Top: Learned solution uθ(x, t) (left) and forward-predicted solution up(x, t) (right) plotted for t = tend as specified in Table 4. Middle left: Learned diffusion function Dϕ(u). Representative results are shown for wPDE ∈ {10−4, 10−1, 103}; dashed black curves denote the true solution or constitutive function and shaded regions represent ±1 standard deviation across ten BINN initialisations. Middle right: Weighted validation losses, showing Ldata (solid) and wPDELPDE (dashed) with shaded regions representing ±1 standard deviation across ten BINN initialisations. Bottom: Relative L2 errors in uθ and up as wPDE varies. Unless stated otherwise, all remaining ADR–BINN hyperparameters take the default values given in Table 3.

Fig 5. Effect of operator network architecture on ADR–BINN performance for the linear diffusion–nonlinear advection equation (Eq. (12)) with additive Gaussian noise of variance σ2 = 0.001. Top: Learned solution uθ(x, t) (left) and forward-predicted solution up(x, t) (right). Middle: Learned constitutive functions Dϕ(u) (left) and Vζ(u) (right) plotted for t = tend as specified in Table 4. Results are shown for operator network architectures (hD,V , nD,V ) ∈ {(1, 1), (4, 1), (4, 4), (4, 32)}; dashed black curves denote the true solution or operators, and shaded regions indicate ±1 standard deviation over ten independent ADR–BINN initialisations. Note that when there is only one hidden layer, an Identity activation function is used in the input layer and a Linear activation function, where Linear(x;W, b) = Linear(x) = xW⊤ + b, where W is the weight matrix and b is the bias vector, is used for the output layer. Bottom: Total validation loss during training for each operator network architecture (left). Mean relative L2 error in the forward-predicted solution up for all sixteen combinations of diffusion and advection network architectures. Unless stated otherwise, all remaining ADR–BINN hyperparameters take the default values given in Table 3.

Fig 6. Effect of mini-batch size, B, on ADR–BINN optimisation and reconstruction accuracy for the diffusion equation (Eq.(3)) with additive Gaussian noise of variance σ2 = 0.001. Top: Learned solution uθ(x, t) (left) and forward-predicted solution up(x, t) (right) plotted for t = tend as specified in Table 4. Middle: Total validation loss during training for B = {10, 40, 160, 640} (left). Median wall-clock training time over ten repetitions for 4000 epochs as a function of batch size; the dashed line shows the fitted inverse relationship (right). Bottom: Relative L2 errors in uθ and up after a fixed training budget of five minutes. Unless stated otherwise, NPDE = NBC = 40 and all remaining hyperparameters take the default values given in Table 3.
